Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Markov Decision Processes

Finite-horizon dynamic programming chooses an action from each state and time, then follows one deterministic successor. How should the recursion change when an action induces a distribution of successors and the decision rule itself may be randomized or depend on history? Stochastic dynamic programming answers by averaging continuation values under a transition kernel.

Decision Rules and Policies¶

Which combinations of state, history, and randomization may a decision rule use when selecting an action?

Before diving into stochastic systems, we need to establish terminology for the different types of strategies a decision maker might employ. In the deterministic setting, we implicitly used feedback controllers of the form u(x,t)u(\mathbf{x}, t)u(x,t). In the stochastic setting, we must be more precise about what information policies can use and how they select actions.

A decision rule is a prescription for action selection in each state at a specified decision epoch. These rules can vary in their complexity based on two main criteria:

  1. Dependence on history: Markovian or History-dependent

  2. Action selection method: Deterministic or Randomized

Markovian decision rules depend only on the current state, while history-dependent rules consider the entire sequence of past states and actions. Formally, a history hth_tht​ at time ttt is:

ht=(s1,a1,…,st−1,at−1,st)h_t = (s_1, a_1, \ldots, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, s_t)ht​=(s1​,a1​,…,st−1​,at−1​,st​)
(1)

The set of all possible histories at time ttt, denoted HtH_tHt​, grows exponentially with ttt:

  • H1=SH_1 = \mathcal{S}H1​=S (just the initial state)

  • H2=S×A×SH_2 = \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{S}H2​=S×A×S

  • Ht=S×(A×S)t−1H_t = \mathcal{S} \times (\mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{S})^{t-1}Ht​=S×(A×S)t−1

Deterministic rules select an action with certainty, while randomized rules specify a probability distribution over the action space.

These classifications lead to four types of decision rules:

  1. Markovian Deterministic (MD): πt:S→As\pi_t: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}_sπt​:S→As​

  2. Markovian Randomized (MR): πt:S→P(As)\pi_t: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}_s)πt​:S→P(As​)

  3. History-dependent Deterministic (HD): πt:Ht→As\pi_t: H_t \rightarrow \mathcal{A}_sπt​:Ht​→As​

  4. History-dependent Randomized (HR): πt:Ht→P(As)\pi_t: H_t \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}_s)πt​:Ht​→P(As​)

where P(As)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}_s)P(As​) denotes the set of probability distributions over As\mathcal{A}_sAs​.

A policy π\boldsymbol{\pi}π is a sequence of decision rules, one for each decision epoch:

π=(π1,π2,...,πN−1)\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi_1, \pi_2, ..., \pi_{N-1})π=(π1​,π2​,...,πN−1​)
(2)

The set of all policies of class KKK (where K∈{HR,HD,MR,MD}K \in \{HR, HD, MR, MD\}K∈{HR,HD,MR,MD}) is denoted as ΠK\Pi^KΠK. These policy classes form a hierarchy:

ΠMD⊂ΠMR⊂ΠHR,ΠMD⊂ΠHD⊂ΠHR\Pi^{MD} \subset \Pi^{MR} \subset \Pi^{HR}, \quad \Pi^{MD} \subset \Pi^{HD} \subset \Pi^{HR}ΠMD⊂ΠMR⊂ΠHR,ΠMD⊂ΠHD⊂ΠHR
(3)

The largest set ΠHR\Pi^{HR}ΠHR contains all possible policies. We ask: under what conditions can we restrict attention to the much simpler set ΠMD\Pi^{MD}ΠMD without loss of optimality?

Notation: rules vs. policies

  • Decision rule (kernel). A map from information to action distributions:

    • Markov, deterministic: πt:S→As\pi_t:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A}_sπt​:S→As​

    • Markov, randomized: πt(⋅∣s)∈Δ(As)\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_s)πt​(⋅∣s)∈Δ(As​)

    • History-dependent: πt(⋅∣ht)∈Δ(Ast)\pi_t(\cdot\mid h_t)\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{s_t})πt​(⋅∣ht​)∈Δ(Ast​​)

  • Policy (sequence). π=(π1,π2,…)\boldsymbol{\pi}=(\pi_1,\pi_2,\ldots)π=(π1​,π2​,…).

  • Stationary policy. π=const(π)\boldsymbol{\pi}=\mathrm{const}(\pi)π=const(π) with πt≡π ∀t\pi_t\equiv\pi \ \forall tπt​≡π ∀t.
    By convention, we identify π\piπ with its stationary policy const(π)\mathrm{const}(\pi)const(π) when no confusion arises.

Stochastic System Dynamics¶

How does a transition kernel replace the single deterministic successor in the finite-horizon model?

In the stochastic setting, our system evolution takes the form:

xt+1=ft(xt,ut,wt)\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = \mathbf{f}_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t)xt+1​=ft​(xt​,ut​,wt​)
(4)

Here, wt\mathbf{w}_twt​ represents a random disturbance or noise term at time ttt due to the inherent uncertainty in the system’s behavior. The stage cost function may also incorporate stochastic influences:

ct(xt,ut,wt)c_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t)ct​(xt​,ut​,wt​)
(5)

In this context, our objective shifts from minimizing a deterministic cost to minimizing the expected total cost:

E[cT(xT)+∑t=1T−1ct(xt,ut,wt)]\mathbb{E}\left[c_\mathrm{T}(\mathbf{x}_T) + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} c_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t)\right]E[cT​(xT​)+t=1∑T−1​ct​(xt​,ut​,wt​)]
(6)

where the expectation is taken over the distributions of the random variables wt\mathbf{w}_twt​. The principle of optimality still holds in the stochastic case, but Bellman’s optimality equation now involves an expectation:

Jk⋆(xk)=min⁡ukEwk[ck(xk,uk,wk)+Jk+1⋆(fk(xk,uk,wk))]J_k^\star(\mathbf{x}_k) = \min_{\mathbf{u}_k} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}_k}\left[c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k) + J_{k+1}^\star(\mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k))\right]Jk⋆​(xk​)=uk​min​Ewk​​[ck​(xk​,uk​,wk​)+Jk+1⋆​(fk​(xk​,uk​,wk​))]
(7)

In practice, this expectation is often computed by discretizing the distribution of wk\mathbf{w}_kwk​ when the set of possible disturbances is very large or even continuous. Let’s say we approximate the distribution with KKK discrete values wki\mathbf{w}_k^iwki​, each occurring with probability pkip_k^ipki​. Then our Bellman equation becomes:

Jk⋆(xk)=min⁡uk∑i=1Kpki(ck(xk,uk,wki)+Jk+1⋆(fk(xk,uk,wki)))J_k^\star(\mathbf{x}_k) = \min_{\mathbf{u}_k} \sum_{i=1}^K p_k^i \left(c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k^i) + J_{k+1}^\star(\mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k^i))\right)Jk⋆​(xk​)=uk​min​i=1∑K​pki​(ck​(xk​,uk​,wki​)+Jk+1⋆​(fk​(xk​,uk​,wki​)))
(8)

Optimality Equations in the Stochastic Setting¶

How is the deterministic continuation value replaced by an expectation over all possible next states?

When dealing with stochastic systems, a central question arises: what information should our control policy use? In the most general case, a policy might use the entire history of observations and actions. However, as we’ll see, the Markovian structure of our problems allows for dramatic simplifications.

Let ht=(s1,a1,s2,a2,…,st−1,at−1,st)h_t = (s_1, a_1, s_2, a_2, \ldots, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, s_t)ht​=(s1​,a1​,s2​,a2​,…,st−1​,at−1​,st​) denote the complete history up to time ttt. In the stochastic setting, the history-based optimality equations become:

ut(ht)=sup⁡a∈Ast{rt(st,a)+∑j∈Spt(j∣st,a) ut+1(ht,a,j)},uN(hN)=rN(sN)u_t(h_t) = \sup_{a\in A_{s_t}}\left\{ r_t(s_t,a) + \sum_{j\in S} p_t(j\mid s_t,a)\, u_{t+1}(h_t,a,j) \right\},\quad u_N(h_N)=r_N(s_N)ut​(ht​)=a∈Ast​​sup​⎩⎨⎧​rt​(st​,a)+j∈S∑​pt​(j∣st​,a)ut+1​(ht​,a,j)⎭⎬⎫​,uN​(hN​)=rN​(sN​)
(9)

where we now explicitly use the transition probabilities pt(j∣st,a)p_t(j|s_t,a)pt​(j∣st​,a) rather than a deterministic dynamics function.

Theorem 1 (Principle of optimality for stochastic systems)

Let ut∗u_t^*ut∗​ be the optimal expected return from epoch ttt onward. Then:

a. ut∗u_t^*ut∗​ satisfies the optimality equations:

ut∗(ht)=sup⁡a∈Ast{rt(st,a)+∑j∈Spt(j∣st,a)ut+1∗(ht,a,j)}u_t^*(h_t) = \sup_{a \in A_{s_t}} \left\{ r_t(s_t, a) + \sum_{j \in S} p_t(j|s_t, a) u_{t+1}^*(h_t, a, j) \right\}ut∗​(ht​)=a∈Ast​​sup​⎩⎨⎧​rt​(st​,a)+j∈S∑​pt​(j∣st​,a)ut+1∗​(ht​,a,j)⎭⎬⎫​
(10)

with boundary condition uN∗(hN)=rN(sN)u_N^*(h_N) = r_N(s_N)uN∗​(hN​)=rN​(sN​).

b. Any policy π∗\pi^*π∗ that selects actions attaining the supremum (or maximum) in the above equation at each history is optimal.

Intuition: This formalizes Bellman’s principle of optimality: “An optimal policy has the property that whatever the initial state and initial decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision.” The recursive structure means that optimal local decisions (choosing the best action at each step) lead to global optimality, even with uncertainty captured by the transition probabilities.

A simplification occurs when we examine these history-based equations more closely. The Markov property of our system dynamics and rewards means that the optimal return actually depends on the history only through the current state:

Proposition 1 (State sufficiency for stochastic MDPs)

In finite-horizon stochastic MDPs with Markovian dynamics and rewards, the optimal return ut∗(ht)u_t^*(h_t)ut∗​(ht​) depends on the history only through the current state sts_tst​. Thus we can write ut∗(ht)=vt∗(st)u_t^*(h_t) = v_t^*(s_t)ut∗​(ht​)=vt∗​(st​) for some function vt∗v_t^*vt∗​ that depends only on state and time.

Proof 1

Following Puterman (1994) Theorem 4.4.2. We proceed by backward induction.

Base case: At the terminal time NNN, we have uN∗(hN)=rN(sN)u_N^*(h_N) = r_N(s_N)uN∗​(hN​)=rN​(sN​) by the boundary condition. Since the terminal reward depends only on the final state sNs_NsN​ and not on how we arrived there, uN∗(hN)=uN∗(sN)u_N^*(h_N) = u_N^*(s_N)uN∗​(hN​)=uN∗​(sN​).

Inductive step: Assume ut+1∗(ht+1)u_{t+1}^*(h_{t+1})ut+1∗​(ht+1​) depends on ht+1h_{t+1}ht+1​ only through st+1s_{t+1}st+1​ for all t+1,…,Nt+1, \ldots, Nt+1,…,N. Then from the optimality equation:

ut∗(ht)=sup⁡a∈Ast{rt(st,a)+∑j∈Spt(j∣st,a)ut+1∗(ht,a,j)}u_t^*(h_t) = \sup_{a \in A_{s_t}} \left\{ r_t(s_t, a) + \sum_{j \in S} p_t(j|s_t, a) u_{t+1}^*(h_t, a, j) \right\}ut∗​(ht​)=a∈Ast​​sup​⎩⎨⎧​rt​(st​,a)+j∈S∑​pt​(j∣st​,a)ut+1∗​(ht​,a,j)⎭⎬⎫​
(11)

By the induction hypothesis, ut+1∗(ht,a,j)u_{t+1}^*(h_t, a, j)ut+1∗​(ht​,a,j) depends only on the next state jjj, so:

ut∗(ht)=sup⁡a∈Ast{rt(st,a)+∑j∈Spt(j∣st,a)ut+1∗(j)}u_t^*(h_t) = \sup_{a \in A_{s_t}} \left\{ r_t(s_t, a) + \sum_{j \in S} p_t(j|s_t, a) u_{t+1}^*(j) \right\}ut∗​(ht​)=a∈Ast​​sup​⎩⎨⎧​rt​(st​,a)+j∈S∑​pt​(j∣st​,a)ut+1∗​(j)⎭⎬⎫​
(12)

Since the expression in brackets depends on hth_tht​ only through the current state sts_tst​ (the rewards and transition probabilities are Markovian), we conclude that ut∗(ht)=ut∗(st)u_t^*(h_t) = u_t^*(s_t)ut∗​(ht​)=ut∗​(st​).

Intuition: The Markov property means that the current state contains all information needed to predict future evolution. The past provides no additional value for decision-making. This result allows us to work with value functions vt∗(s)v_t^*(s)vt∗​(s) indexed only by state and time, dramatically simplifying both theory and computation.

This state-sufficiency result, combined with the fact that randomization never helps when maximizing expected returns, leads to a dramatic simplification of the policy space:

Theorem 2 (Policy reduction for stochastic MDPs)

For finite-horizon stochastic MDPs with finite state and action sets:

sup⁡π∈ΠHRvπ(s,t)=max⁡π∈ΠMDvπ(s,t)\sup_{\pi \in \Pi^{\mathrm{HR}}} v_\pi(s,t) = \max_{\pi \in \Pi^{\mathrm{MD}}} v_\pi(s,t)π∈ΠHRsup​vπ​(s,t)=π∈ΠMDmax​vπ​(s,t)
(13)

That is, there exists an optimal policy that is both deterministic and Markovian.

Proof 2

Sketch following Puterman (1994) Lemma 4.3.1 and Theorem 4.4.2. First, Lemma 4.3.1 shows that for any function www and any distribution qqq over actions, sup⁡aw(a)≥∑aq(a)w(a)\sup_a w(a) \ge \sum_a q(a) w(a)supa​w(a)≥∑a​q(a)w(a). Thus randomization cannot improve the expected value over choosing a single maximizing action. Second, by state sufficiency (Proposition Proposition 1 and Puterman (1994) Thm. 4.4.2(a)), the optimal return depends on the history only through (st,t)(s_t,t)(st​,t). Therefore, selecting at each (st,t)(s_t,t)(st​,t) an action that attains the maximum yields a deterministic Markov decision rule which is optimal whenever the maximum is attained. If only a supremum exists, ε\varepsilonε-optimal selectors exist by choosing actions within ε\varepsilonε of the supremum (see Puterman (1994) Thm. 4.3.4).

Intuition: Even in stochastic systems, randomization in the policy doesn’t help when maximizing expected returns: you should always choose the action with the highest expected value. Combined with state sufficiency, this means simple state-to-action mappings are optimal.

These results justify focusing on deterministic Markov policies and lead to the backward recursion algorithm for stochastic systems:

Algorithm 1 (Backward Recursion for Stochastic Dynamic Programming)

Input: Terminal cost function cT(⋅)c_\mathrm{T}(\cdot)cT​(⋅), stage cost functions ct(⋅,⋅,⋅)c_t(\cdot, \cdot, \cdot)ct​(⋅,⋅,⋅), system dynamics ft(⋅,⋅,⋅)\mathbf{f}_t(\cdot, \cdot, \cdot)ft​(⋅,⋅,⋅), time horizon T\mathrm{T}T, disturbance distributions

Output: Optimal value functions Jt⋆(⋅)J_t^\star(\cdot)Jt⋆​(⋅) and optimal control policies πt⋆(⋅)\pi_t^\star(\cdot)πt⋆​(⋅) for t=1,…,Tt = 1, \ldots, Tt=1,…,T

  1. Initialize JT⋆(x)=cT(x)J_T^\star(\mathbf{x}) = c_\mathrm{T}(\mathbf{x})JT⋆​(x)=cT​(x) for all x\mathbf{x}x in the state space

  2. For t=T−1,T−2,…,1t = T-1, T-2, \ldots, 1t=T−1,T−2,…,1:

    1. For each state x\mathbf{x}x in the state space:

      1. Compute Jt⋆(x)=min⁡uEwt[ct(x,u,wt)+Jt+1⋆(ft(x,u,wt))]J_t^\star(\mathbf{x}) = \min_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}_t}\left[c_t(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}_t) + J_{t+1}^\star(\mathbf{f}_t(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}_t))\right]Jt⋆​(x)=minu​Ewt​​[ct​(x,u,wt​)+Jt+1⋆​(ft​(x,u,wt​))]

      2. Compute πt⋆(x)=arg⁡min⁡uEwt[ct(x,u,wt)+Jt+1⋆(ft(x,u,wt))]\pi_t^\star(\mathbf{x}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}_t}\left[c_t(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}_t) + J_{t+1}^\star(\mathbf{f}_t(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}_t))\right]πt⋆​(x)=argminu​Ewt​​[ct​(x,u,wt​)+Jt+1⋆​(ft​(x,u,wt​))]

    2. End For

  3. End For

  4. Return Jt⋆(⋅)J_t^\star(\cdot)Jt⋆​(⋅), πt⋆(⋅)\pi_t^\star(\cdot)πt⋆​(⋅) for t=1,…,Tt = 1, \ldots, Tt=1,…,T

While SDP provides us with a framework for handling uncertainty, it makes the curse of dimensionality even more difficult to handle in practice. Both the state space and the disturbance space must be discretized. This can lead to a combinatorial explosion in the number of scenarios to be evaluated at each stage.

However, just as we tackled the challenges of continuous state spaces with discretization and interpolation, we can devise efficient methods to handle the additional complexity of evaluating expectations. This problem essentially becomes one of numerical integration. When the set of disturbances is continuous (as is often the case with continuous state spaces), we enter a domain where numerical quadrature methods could be applied. But these methods tend to scale poorly as the number of dimensions grows. This is where more efficient techniques, often rooted in Monte Carlo methods, come into play. Two ingredients tackle the curse of dimensionality:

  1. Function approximation (through discretization, interpolation, neural networks, etc.)

  2. Monte Carlo integration (simulation)

These two elements essentially distill the key ingredients of machine learning, which is the direction we’ll be exploring in this course.

Example: Reservoir Operation with Random Inflows¶

How does the reservoir policy change when each week’s release must be chosen before that week’s inflow is known?

The previous chapter operated a seasonal hydroelectric reservoir against an inflow forecast and treated the forecast as exact. Its policy refills the reservoir after the spring freshet, holds it at capacity from September to late November, and releases exactly the forecast inflow in each of those weeks. That plan is only as good as the forecast: in a week wetter than forecast, the reservoir is already full and the extra water goes over the spillway. Stochastic dynamic programming has long been used to compute reservoir operating policies that account for this risk Stedinger et al., 1984. We make the inflow random and keep every other element of the deterministic model: 52 weekly stages, the storage and release limits, the head h(x)h(x)h(x), the price ptp_tpt​ and the terminal value.

Let wˉt\bar w_twˉt​ denote the forecast of the previous chapter. The inflow in week ttt is

wt=ξt wˉt,ξt={0.6with probability 1/4,1.0with probability 1/2,1.4with probability 1/4,w_t = \xi_t\,\bar w_t, \qquad \xi_t = \begin{cases} 0.6 & \text{with probability } 1/4, \\ 1.0 & \text{with probability } 1/2, \\ 1.4 & \text{with probability } 1/4, \end{cases}wt​=ξt​wˉt​,ξt​=⎩⎨⎧​0.61.01.4​with probability 1/4,with probability 1/2,with probability 1/4,​
(14)

where the factors ξ0,…,ξ51\xi_0, \ldots, \xi_{51}ξ0​,…,ξ51​ are independent. The mean inflow equals the forecast, and one week in four is 40% wetter than forecast. The inflow plays the role of the disturbance wt\mathbf{w}_twt​ in the stochastic dynamics above. Because the factors are independent, past inflows carry no information about the next one, and storage alone remains a sufficient state, as in Proposition 1.

The operator sets the release utu_tut​ at the start of the week, before the inflow arrives. In a dry week the requested release can exceed the water available above dead storage. The turbines then stop when the level reaches dead storage, so the volume actually released is

u~t=min⁡{ut, xt+wt−xmin⁡}.\tilde u_t = \min\{u_t,\ x_t + w_t - x_{\min}\}.u~t​=min{ut​, xt​+wt​−xmin​}.
(15)

Storage evolves as xt+1=min⁡{xt+wt−u~t, xˉ}x_{t+1} = \min\{x_t + w_t - \tilde u_t,\ \bar x\}xt+1​=min{xt​+wt​−u~t​, xˉ}, and the week earns pt κ h(xt) u~tp_t\,\kappa\,h(x_t)\,\tilde u_tpt​κh(xt​)u~t​. Both the successor and the revenue now depend on the disturbance, as ft(xt,ut,wt)\mathbf{f}_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t)ft​(xt​,ut​,wt​) and ct(xt,ut,wt)c_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t)ct​(xt​,ut​,wt​) do in the general formulation. Writing ξk\xi^kξk for the three factors and qkq_kqk​ for their probabilities, Bellman’s equation reads

Jt⋆(x)=max⁡umin⁡≤u≤umax⁡∑k=13qk[ pt κ h(x) u~k+Jt+1⋆(min⁡{x+ξkwˉt−u~k, xˉ})],u~k=min⁡{u, x+ξkwˉt−xmin⁡},J_t^\star(x) = \max_{u_{\min} \le u \le u_{\max}} \sum_{k=1}^{3} q_k \Big[\, p_t\,\kappa\,h(x)\,\tilde u^k + J_{t+1}^\star\big(\min\{x + \xi^k \bar w_t - \tilde u^k,\ \bar x\}\big) \Big], \qquad \tilde u^k = \min\{u,\ x + \xi^k \bar w_t - x_{\min}\},Jt⋆​(x)=umin​≤u≤umax​max​k=1∑3​qk​[pt​κh(x)u~k+Jt+1⋆​(min{x+ξkwˉt​−u~k, xˉ})],u~k=min{u, x+ξkwˉt​−xmin​},
(16)

with the terminal value JT⋆(x)=pT κ h(x) (x−xmin⁡)J_T^\star(x) = p_T\,\kappa\,h(x)\,(x - x_{\min})JT⋆​(x)=pT​κh(x)(x−xmin​) as before. The expectation sits inside the maximum because a single release has to serve all three inflows.

The code below changes the deterministic solver in two places. The bracket is averaged over the three inflows before the maximum over releases is taken. And the successors x+0.6 wˉt−ux + 0.6\,\bar w_t - ux+0.6wˉt​−u and x+1.4 wˉt−ux + 1.4\,\bar w_t - ux+1.4wˉt​−u are in general no longer multiples of the 10 hm³ grid step, so Jt+1⋆J_{t+1}^\starJt+1⋆​ is evaluated between grid points by linear interpolation, as in the interpolation section of the previous chapter. Given the single factor 1 with probability 1, the same function solves the deterministic problem and returns its 74.1 M$ from 1100 hm³; with a known inflow, stopping a release at dead storage is the same as forbidding it. This is the certainty-equivalent problem: the random inflow is replaced by its mean, and the resulting policy is applied as if the forecast were exact. The last lines operate both policies for 2000 simulated years, on the same inflow sequences.

import numpy as np

# The deterministic model of the previous chapter.
T = 52
weeks = np.arange(T)
w_bar = 60 + 340 * np.exp(-((weeks - 19) / 3.5) ** 2) + 60 * np.exp(-((weeks - 43) / 4) ** 2)
w_bar = 10 * np.round(w_bar / 10)                    # inflow forecast (hm³/week)
p = 60 + 30 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (weeks - 5) / 52)   # price ($/MWh)
x_min, x_max = 200, 2000
u_min, u_max = 30, 250
kappa, p_T = 2.45, 50

def head(x):
    return 40 + 40 * np.sqrt(x / x_max)

def terminal_value(x):
    return p_T * kappa * head(x) * (x - x_min)

dx = 10
X = np.arange(x_min, x_max + dx, dx)
U = np.arange(u_min, u_max + dx, dx)

# Random inflow w_t = xi_t * w_bar_t, with xi_t drawn independently each week.
factors = np.array([0.6, 1.0, 1.4])
probs = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.25])

def solve(factors, probs):
    J = np.zeros((T + 1, len(X)))
    policy = np.zeros((T, len(X)))
    J[T] = terminal_value(X)
    x, u = X[:, None], U[None, :]                     # all (storage, release) pairs
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        value = np.zeros((len(X), len(U)))
        for factor, prob in zip(factors, probs):      # expectation over the inflow...
            inflow = factor * w_bar[t]
            release = np.minimum(u, x + inflow - x_min)       # turbines stop at dead storage
            x_next = np.minimum(x + inflow - release, x_max)  # water above capacity spills
            value += prob * (p[t] * kappa * head(x) * release
                             + np.interp(x_next, X, J[t + 1]))
        J[t] = value.max(axis=1)                      # ...inside the maximum over releases
        policy[t] = U[value.argmax(axis=1)]
    return J, policy

def simulate(policy, years, x0):
    """Operate the reservoir for many years at once: one row of factors per year."""
    x = np.full(len(years), float(x0))
    storage, revenue, spill = [x], 0.0, 0.0
    for t in range(T):
        inflow = years[:, t] * w_bar[t]
        requested = policy[t, np.round((x - x_min) / dx).astype(int)]
        release = np.minimum(requested, x + inflow - x_min)
        revenue = revenue + p[t] * kappa * head(x) * release
        spill = spill + np.maximum(x + inflow - release - x_max, 0)
        x = np.minimum(x + inflow - release, x_max)
        storage.append(x)
    return np.array(storage), revenue + terminal_value(x), spill

J_ce, policy_ce = solve([1.0], [1.0])         # certainty equivalent: inflow = forecast
J_sto, policy_sto = solve(factors, probs)     # stochastic dynamic programming

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
years = rng.choice(factors, size=(2000, T), p=probs)   # the same inflows for both policies
i0 = np.searchsorted(X, 1100)
results = {}
for name, J, policy in (("certainty equivalent", J_ce, policy_ce),
                        ("stochastic", J_sto, policy_sto)):
    storage, revenue, spill = simulate(policy, years, x0=1100)
    results[name] = (storage, revenue, spill)
    print(f"{name:<21} predicted {J[0, i0] / 1e6:5.2f} M$   simulated {revenue.mean() / 1e6:5.2f} M$"
          f"   spill {spill.mean():3.0f} hm³/year")
certainty equivalent  predicted 74.06 M$   simulated 73.05 M$   spill  85 hm³/year
stochastic            predicted 73.75 M$   simulated 73.74 M$   spill   1 hm³/year

The two backward passes predict different things. The certainty-equivalent pass predicts 74.06 M$, the revenue its policy would earn if every week’s inflow matched the forecast, which never happens. On the simulated inflows the same policy earns 73.05 M$ on average, about 1 M$ less, and spills water in 96% of the years. At a water value of about 11 k$ per hm³, the 85 hm³ it spills each year account for most of the shortfall. The stochastic pass predicts 73.75 M$, and the simulation agrees within its standard error of 0.06 M$. This agreement is expected: J0⋆(1100)J_0^\star(1100)J0⋆​(1100) is the expected revenue of the stochastic policy under the inflow model, and the average over simulated years estimates the same expectation.

On the same inflows, the stochastic policy earns 0.68 M$ more per year than the certainty-equivalent policy. Stochastic programming calls this difference the value of the stochastic solution Birge & Louveaux, 2011. It is small next to the total revenue, but most of that revenue comes from water that any rule would sell. In the deterministic model, running the river without storing anything earned 66.8 M$, and managing the storage added 7.3 M$. The loss from ignoring the inflow uncertainty is about a tenth of that amount.

from pathlib import Path
import sys

code_directory = Path.cwd() / "code"
if str(code_directory) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(code_directory))

from hydro_reservoir_stochastic import (
    make_stochastic_comparison_figure,
    make_stochastic_policy_figure,

water_value_ce = np.gradient(J_ce, dx, axis=1)    # dJ_t/dx on the grid, $ per hm³
water_value_sto = np.gradient(J_sto, dx, axis=1)
storage_ce, revenue_ce, spill_ce = results["certainty equivalent"]
storage_sto, revenue_sto, spill_sto = results["stochastic"]

Because both policies face the same inflows, the gain can be measured year by year, as in the right panel of Figure 1. Its mean has a standard error of 0.01 M$, against 0.06 M$ for either mean revenue: a wet or dry year raises or lowers the revenue of both policies alike, and this common variation cancels in the difference. Evaluating competing policies on the same random inputs is a variance-reduction technique known as common random numbers. The stochastic policy earns more in 87% of the years. The other years have dry autumns, in which the certainty-equivalent policy spills little and the margin kept by the stochastic policy turns out to be unnecessary.

The gain comes almost entirely from the autumn, shown in the left panel. The certainty-equivalent policy refills the reservoir to capacity in September and holds it there, releasing the forecast inflow each week, so every week wetter than forecast spills. The stochastic policy stops about 50 hm³ below capacity. In late October the forecast inflow is 120 hm³ per week, and the wettest week brings 0.4×120=480.4 \times 120 = 480.4×120=48 hm³ more than forecast. The policy keeps exactly enough room to absorb it.

The size of this margin follows from the comparison that explained the deterministic policy in the previous chapter: the turbines run when releasing one more hm³, worth pt κ h(x)p_t\,\kappa\,h(x)pt​κh(x), earns more than keeping it, worth the water value ∂Jt+1⋆/∂x\partial J_{t+1}^\star/\partial x∂Jt+1⋆​/∂x at the next storage. With random inflow, the second term becomes an average over the three successors xt+1kx_{t+1}^kxt+1k​. For an inflow that fills the reservoir, an hm³ kept this week spills and adds nothing next week, so those successors drop out of the average. As long as the release is not cut short at dead storage, the slope ∂Qt/∂u\partial Q_t/\partial u∂Qt​/∂u from the previous chapter becomes

pt κ h(x)  −  ∑k: xt+1k<xˉqk ∂Jt+1⋆∂x(xt+1k).p_t\,\kappa\,h(x) \;-\; \sum_{k:\ x_{t+1}^k < \bar x} q_k\, \frac{\partial J_{t+1}^\star}{\partial x}\big(x_{t+1}^k\big).pt​κh(x)−k: xt+1k​<xˉ∑​qk​∂x∂Jt+1⋆​​(xt+1k​).
(17)

The rule becomes: run the turbines when the price exceeds the expected value of the water kept, counting water that would spill as worth nothing. In late October, near capacity, one hm³ earns about 10.3 k$ if released and has a water value of about 11.2 k$ if kept. Below the margin, the kept hm³ never spills, so keeping it is worth more. Above the margin, it spills in the wettest week, with probability 1/4, and its expected value falls to 0.75×11.2=8.40.75 \times 11.2 = 8.40.75×11.2=8.4 k$, less than the 10.3 k$ from releasing it. The policy therefore holds the storage level from which the wettest week just fills the reservoir. In the deterministic model the inflow is known, so the policy can fill the reservoir to capacity without spilling.

The same averaging changes the water value. The right panel of Figure 2 shows it in week 14, early April, when the freshet begins. In the certainty-equivalent model it drops abruptly at 1770 hm³: from that level on, the forecast freshet fills the reservoir, and any additional hm³ is certain to spill. In the stochastic model the drop is spread from about 1100 hm³ to capacity. An additional hm³ spills only if the freshet is wet enough, and the probability of such a freshet rises gradually with storage. More generally, each Jt⋆J_t^\starJt⋆​ averages Jt+1⋆J_{t+1}^\starJt+1⋆​ over three successors, and this averaging smooths the kinks of the deterministic value function at every step of the recursion.

The white curves in the left panel are 40 simulated years. In the deterministic model a single path described the operation of the policy; here each year follows its own. The paths spread out in January and February, while the policy releases the minimum and storage follows the random inflow. They come back together at the end of the winter drawdown, when every year reaches low storage before the freshet, spread again during the freshet, whose volume differs from year to year, and converge in autumn toward the level below capacity where the policy holds them. The outcome of a policy under uncertainty is a distribution, and estimating it takes many simulated trajectories. The same holds for the reinforcement learning methods of later chapters: one good trajectory does not show that a policy is good.

Question. If the operator could see each week’s inflow before choosing the release, would the expected revenue from 1100 hm³ be above or below 73.75 M$? Which lines of solve would change?

Answer

Above, or at least equal. Seeing the inflow first allows a different release for each of the three inflows, and choosing the same release for all three remains possible, so the maximum cannot decrease. In Bellman’s equation the maximum moves inside the expectation, Jt⋆(x)=∑kqkmax⁡u[ ⋯ ]J_t^\star(x) = \sum_k q_k \max_u [\,\cdots]Jt⋆​(x)=∑k​qk​maxu​[⋯]. In solve, each term is maximized over releases before it is added, value += prob * (...).max(axis=1) with value a vector over storage levels, and J[t] = value. The policy then depends on the inflow as well as on the storage. The expected revenue becomes 74.01 M$, so knowing each week’s inflow in advance is worth 0.26 M$ per year.

Question. In this model the inflow factor is drawn independently each week, so a wet April says nothing about May. Real freshets tend to be wet or dry for weeks at a time, because they melt from a single snowpack. What would the state have to contain for the backward recursion to remain valid, and what would that cost?

Answer

With correlated inflows, storage is no longer a sufficient state: the distribution of next week’s inflow depends on past inflows, and the argument of Proposition 1 no longer applies to storage alone. If the factor follows a Markov chain, adding last week’s factor to the state restores it. The state becomes (xt,ξt−1)(x_t, \xi_{t-1})(xt​,ξt−1​), with 181×3=543181 \times 3 = 543181×3=543 grid points instead of 181, and the expectation uses the transition probabilities out of ξt−1\xi_{t-1}ξt−1​. A measured snowpack would be a continuous second state variable with its own grid. Each such variable multiplies the size of the grid, which is the curse of dimensionality again. A common alternative is to re-solve a deterministic problem every week with an updated forecast, as in receding-horizon control.

Markov Decision Process Formulation¶

Which state, action, transition, reward, and horizon objects define the common finite MDP representation?

Rather than expressing the stochasticity in our system through a disturbance term as a parameter to a deterministic difference equation, we often work with an alternative representation (more common in operations research) which uses the Markov Decision Process formulation. The idea is that when we model our system in this way with the disturbance term being drawn independently of the previous stages, the induced trajectories are those of a Markov chain. Hence, we can re-cast our control problem in that language, leading to the so-called Markov Decision Process framework in which we express the system dynamics in terms of transition probabilities rather than explicit state equations. In this framework, we express the probability that the system is in a given state using the transition probability function:

pt(xt+1∣xt,ut)p_t(\mathbf{x}_{t+1} | \mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t)pt​(xt+1​∣xt​,ut​)
(18)

This function gives the probability of transitioning to state xt+1\mathbf{x}_{t+1}xt+1​ at time t+1t+1t+1, given that the system is in state xt\mathbf{x}_txt​ and action ut\mathbf{u}_tut​ is taken at time ttt. Therefore, ptp_tpt​ specifies a conditional probability distribution over the next states: namely, the sum (for discrete state spaces) or integral over the next state should be 1.

Given the control theory formulation of our problem via a deterministic dynamics function and a noise term, we can derive the corresponding transition probability function through the following relationship:

pt(xt+1∣xt,ut)=P(Wt∈{w∈W:xt+1=ft(xt,ut,w)})=∑{w∈W:xt+1=ft(xt,ut,w)}qt(w)\begin{aligned} p_t(\mathbf{x}_{t+1} | \mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t) &= \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{W}_t \in \left\{\mathbf{w} \in \mathbf{W}: \mathbf{x}_{t+1} = f_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w})\right\}) \\ &= \sum_{\left\{\mathbf{w} \in \mathbf{W}: \mathbf{x}_{t+1} = f_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w})\right\}} q_t(\mathbf{w}) \end{aligned}pt​(xt+1​∣xt​,ut​)​=P(Wt​∈{w∈W:xt+1​=ft​(xt​,ut​,w)})={w∈W:xt+1​=ft​(xt​,ut​,w)}∑​qt​(w)​
(19)

Here, qt(w)q_t(\mathbf{w})qt​(w) represents the probability density or mass function of the disturbance Wt\mathbf{W}_tWt​ (assuming discrete state spaces). When dealing with continuous spaces, the above expression simply contains an integral rather than a summation.

For a system with deterministic dynamics and no disturbance, the transition probabilities become much simpler and can be expressed using the indicator function. Given a deterministic system with dynamics:

xt+1=ft(xt,ut)\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = f_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t)xt+1​=ft​(xt​,ut​)
(20)

The transition probability function can be expressed as:

pt(xt+1∣xt,ut)={1if xt+1=ft(xt,ut)0otherwisep_t(\mathbf{x}_{t+1} | \mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \mathbf{x}_{t+1} = f_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}pt​(xt+1​∣xt​,ut​)={10​if xt+1​=ft​(xt​,ut​)otherwise​
(21)

With this transition probability function, we can recast our Bellman optimality equation:

Jt⋆(xt)=max⁡ut∈U{ct(xt,ut)+∑xt+1pt(xt+1∣xt,ut)Jt+1⋆(xt+1)}J_t^\star(\mathbf{x}_t) = \max_{\mathbf{u}_t \in \mathbf{U}} \left\{ c_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t) + \sum_{\mathbf{x}_{t+1}} p_t(\mathbf{x}_{t+1} | \mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t) J_{t+1}^\star(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}) \right\}Jt⋆​(xt​)=ut​∈Umax​{ct​(xt​,ut​)+xt+1​∑​pt​(xt+1​∣xt​,ut​)Jt+1⋆​(xt+1​)}
(22)

Here, c(xt,ut){c}(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t)c(xt​,ut​) represents the expected immediate reward (or negative cost) when in state xt\mathbf{x}_txt​ and taking action ut\mathbf{u}_tut​ at time ttt. The summation term computes the expected optimal value for the future states, weighted by their transition probabilities.

This formulation offers several advantages:

  1. It makes the Markovian nature of the problem explicit: the future state depends only on the current state and action, not on the history of states and actions.

  2. For discrete-state problems, the entire system dynamics can be specified by a set of transition matrices, one for each possible action.

  3. It allows us to bridge the gap with the wealth of methods in the field of probabilistic graphical models and statistical machine learning techniques for modelling and analysis.

Notation in Operations Reseach¶

How do equivalent reward, cost, transition, and policy conventions map across reinforcement learning and operations research?

The presentation above was intended to bridge the gap between the control-theoretic perspective and the world of closed-loop control through the idea of determining the value function of a parametric optimal control problem. We then saw how the backward induction procedure was applicable to both the deterministic and stochastic cases by taking the expectation over the disturbance variable. We then said that we can alternatively work with a representation of our system where instead of writing our model as a deterministic dynamics function taking a disturbance as an input, we would rather work directly via its transition probability function, which gives rise to the Markov chain interpretation of our system in simulation.

Note that the notation used in control theory tends to differ from that found in operations research communities, in which the field of dynamic programming flourished. We summarize those (purely notational) differences in this section.

In operations research, the system state at each decision epoch is typically denoted by s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S, where SSS is the set of possible system states. When the system is in state sss, the decision maker may choose an action aaa from the set of allowable actions As\mathcal{A}_sAs​. The union of all action sets is denoted as A=⋃s∈SAs\mathcal{A} = \bigcup_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \mathcal{A}_sA=⋃s∈S​As​.

The dynamics of the system are described by a transition probability function pt(j∣s,a)p_t(j | s, a)pt​(j∣s,a), which represents the probability of transitioning to state j∈Sj \in \mathcal{S}j∈S at time t+1t+1t+1, given that the system is in state sss at time ttt and action a∈Asa \in \mathcal{A}_sa∈As​ is chosen. This transition probability function satisfies:

∑j∈Spt(j∣s,a)=1\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p_t(j | s, a) = 1j∈S∑​pt​(j∣s,a)=1
(23)

It’s worth noting that in operations research, we typically work with reward maximization rather than cost minimization, which is more common in control theory. However, we can easily switch between these perspectives by simply negating the quantity. That is, maximizing a reward function is equivalent to minimizing its negative, which we would then call a cost function.

The reward function is denoted by rt(s,a)r_t(s, a)rt​(s,a), representing the reward received at time ttt when the system is in state sss and action aaa is taken. In some cases, the reward may also depend on the next state, in which case it is denoted as rt(s,a,j)r_t(s, a, j)rt​(s,a,j). The expected reward can then be computed as:

rt(s,a)=∑j∈Srt(s,a,j)pt(j∣s,a)r_t(s, a) = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} r_t(s, a, j) p_t(j | s, a)rt​(s,a)=j∈S∑​rt​(s,a,j)pt​(j∣s,a)
(24)

Combined together, these elements specify a Markov decision process, which is fully described by the tuple:

{T,S,As,pt(⋅∣s,a),rt(s,a)}\{T, S, \mathcal{A}_s, p_t(\cdot | s, a), r_t(s, a)\}{T,S,As​,pt​(⋅∣s,a),rt​(s,a)}
(25)

where T\mathrm{T}T represents the set of decision epochs (the horizon).

What is an Optimal Policy?¶

Against which competing policy class and initial states must a policy be compared before it can be called optimal?

Let’s go back to the starting point and define what it means for a policy to be optimal in a Markov Decision Problem. For this, we will be considering different possible search spaces (policy classes) and comparing policies based on the ordering of their value from any possible start state. The value of a policy π\boldsymbol{\pi}π (optimal or not) is defined as the expected total reward obtained by following that policy from a given starting state. Formally, for a finite-horizon MDP with NNN decision epochs, we define the value function vπ(s,t)v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s, t)vπ(s,t) as:

vπ(s,t)≜E[∑k=tN−1rt(Sk,Ak)+rN(SN)∣St=s]v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s, t) \triangleq \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=t}^{N-1} r_t(S_k, A_k) + r_N(S_N) \mid S_t = s\right]vπ(s,t)≜E[k=t∑N−1​rt​(Sk​,Ak​)+rN​(SN​)∣St​=s]
(26)

where StS_tSt​ is the state at time ttt, AtA_tAt​ is the action taken at time ttt, and rtr_trt​ is the reward function. For simplicity, we write vπ(s)v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)vπ(s) to denote vπ(s,1)v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s, 1)vπ(s,1), the value of following policy π\boldsymbol{\pi}π from state sss at the first stage over the entire horizon NNN.

In finite-horizon MDPs, our goal is to identify an optimal policy, denoted by π∗\boldsymbol{\pi}^*π∗, that maximizes total expected reward over the horizon NNN. Specifically:

vπ∗(s)≥vπ(s),∀s∈S,∀π∈ΠHRv^{\boldsymbol{\pi}^*}(s) \geq v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s), \quad \forall s \in \mathcal{S}, \quad \forall \boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\text{HR}}vπ∗(s)≥vπ(s),∀s∈S,∀π∈ΠHR
(27)

We call π∗\boldsymbol{\pi}^*π∗ an optimal policy because it yields the highest possible value across all states and all policies within the policy class ΠHR\Pi^{\text{HR}}ΠHR. We denote by v∗v^*v∗ the maximum value achievable by any policy:

v∗(s)=max⁡π∈ΠHRvπ(s),∀s∈Sv^*(s) = \max_{\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\text{HR}}} v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s), \quad \forall s \in \mathcal{S}v∗(s)=π∈ΠHRmax​vπ(s),∀s∈S
(28)

In reinforcement learning literature, v∗v^*v∗ is typically referred to as the “optimal value function,” while in some operations research references, it might be called the “value of an MDP.” An optimal policy π∗\boldsymbol{\pi}^*π∗ is one for which its value function equals the optimal value function:

vπ∗(s)=v∗(s),∀s∈Sv^{\boldsymbol{\pi}^*}(s) = v^*(s), \quad \forall s \in \mathcal{S}vπ∗(s)=v∗(s),∀s∈S
(29)

This notion of optimality applies to every state. Policies optimal in this sense are sometimes called “uniformly optimal policies.” A weaker notion of optimality, often encountered in reinforcement learning practice, is optimality with respect to an initial distribution of states. In this case, we seek a policy π∈ΠHR\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\text{HR}}π∈ΠHR that maximizes:

∑s∈Svπ(s)P1(S1=s)\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) P_1(S_1 = s)s∈S∑​vπ(s)P1​(S1​=s)
(30)

where P1(S1=s)P_1(S_1 = s)P1​(S1​=s) is the probability of starting in state sss.

Both definitions rank policies, and the ranking has two ingredients that are modeling choices rather than consequences of the dynamics.

The first is the order itself. Uniform optimality compares value functions state by state: π\boldsymbol{\pi}π is at least as good as π′\boldsymbol{\pi}'π′ when vπ(s)≥vπ′(s)v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) \ge v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}'}(s)vπ(s)≥vπ′(s) for every s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S. This is a partial order. Two policies can be incomparable, each better than the other from some initial state. The existence of a policy that dominates all others in this order is therefore a result to be proved, not an assumption, and the backward induction algorithm below supplies the proof for finite horizons.

The second is the expectation. With noise, a policy induces a distribution over total rewards from each state, and a ranking needs one number per distribution. Taking the mean is the classical answer of expected utility theory, going back to von Neumann and Morgenstern: preferences over uncertain outcomes that satisfy a few consistency axioms can be represented by the expectation of a utility. Using the reward itself as the utility makes the decision maker risk neutral. Two policies with the same mean are equally good, however different their spreads or worst cases. A reservoir operator who must avoid spilling in a wet year may not accept that trade. Risk-sensitive formulations replace the mean by another functional of the distribution, for example the conditional value at risk (CVaR), the mean of the worst α\alphaα-fraction of outcomes. Such criteria lead to different Bellman equations, and some of them no longer decompose stage by stage. This book keeps the expectation throughout.

The maximum value can be achieved by searching over the space of deterministic Markovian Policies. Consequently:

v∗(s)=max⁡π∈ΠHRvπ(s)=max⁡π∈ΠMDvπ(s),s∈Sv^*(s) = \max_{\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\mathrm{HR}}} v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = \max _{\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{M D}} v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s), \quad s \in Sv∗(s)=π∈ΠHRmax​vπ(s)=π∈ΠMDmax​vπ(s),s∈S
(31)

This equality significantly simplifies the computational complexity of our algorithms, as the search problem can now be decomposed into NNN sub-problems in which we only have to search over the set of possible actions. This is the backward induction algorithm, which we present a second time, but departing this time from the control-theoretic notation and using the MDP formalism:

Algorithm 2 (Backward Induction)

Input: State space SSS, Action space AAA, Transition probabilities ptp_tpt​, Reward function rtr_trt​, Time horizon NNN

Output: Optimal value functions v∗v^*v∗ and optimal action sets As,t∗A^*_{s,t}As,t∗​

  1. Initialize:

    • Set t=Nt = Nt=N

    • For all s∈Ss \in Ss∈S:

      v∗(s,N)=rN(s)v^*(s, N) = r_N(s)v∗(s,N)=rN​(s)
      (32)

  2. For t=N−1t = N-1t=N−1 to 1:

    • For each s∈Ss \in Ss∈S: a. Compute the optimal value function:

      v∗(s,t)=max⁡a∈As{rt(s,a)+Es′∼pt(⋅∣s,a)[v∗(s′,t+1)]}v^*(s, t) = \max_{a \in A_s} \left\{r_t(s, a) + \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim p_t(\cdot | s, a)}\left[v^*(s', t+1)\right]\right\}v∗(s,t)=a∈As​max​{rt​(s,a)+Es′∼pt​(⋅∣s,a)​[v∗(s′,t+1)]}
      (33)

      b. Determine the set of optimal actions:

      As,t∗=arg⁡max⁡a∈As{rt(s,a)+Es′∼pt(⋅∣s,a)[v∗(s′,t+1)]}A_{s,t}^* = \arg\max_{a \in A_s} \left\{r_t(s, a) + \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim p_t(\cdot | s, a)}\left[v^*(s', t+1)\right]\right\}As,t∗​=arga∈As​max​{rt​(s,a)+Es′∼pt​(⋅∣s,a)​[v∗(s′,t+1)]}
      (34)

  3. Return the optimal value functions v∗(s,t)v^*(s, t)v∗(s,t) and optimal action sets As,t∗A_{s,t}^*As,t∗​ for all ttt and sss

When SSS is finite, the expectation is the sum ∑s′∈Spt(s′∣s,a) v∗(s′,t+1)\sum_{s' \in S} p_t(s' | s, a)\, v^*(s', t+1)∑s′∈S​pt​(s′∣s,a)v∗(s′,t+1). Writing it as an expectation makes the connection with the stochastic dynamic program from earlier in this chapter explicit: Es′∼pt(⋅∣s,a)\mathbb{E}_{s' \sim p_t(\cdot|s,a)}Es′∼pt​(⋅∣s,a)​ plays the role of Ewt\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}_t}Ewt​​, with the noise absorbed into the transition kernel.

Note that the same procedure can also be used for finding the value of a policy with minor changes;

Algorithm 3 (Policy Evaluation)

Input:

  • State space SSS

  • Action space AAA

  • Transition probabilities ptp_tpt​

Example: Steering Antibiotic Resistance¶

Can a sequence of drugs push a bacterial population away from its most resistant form, and how much does it help to look at the population before choosing each drug?

Many bacteria resist penicillin-like drugs (the β-lactams) by producing an enzyme, β-lactamase, that breaks the drug down. A few point mutations in the enzyme’s gene change which drugs it can break down. Mira et al. (2015) built all 16 combinations of four such mutations (M69L, E104K, G238S and N276D) in the TEM enzyme of E. coli and measured the growth rate of each strain under 15 β-lactams. Each drug therefore defines a fitness landscape: a growth rate for every genotype. The landscapes disagree. A genotype that grows fastest under one drug can be among the slowest under another, so a drug given now changes where evolution goes under the next one. Nichol et al. (2015) used this to steer evolution: give one to three steering drugs before the final treatment, chosen so that the population is unlikely to end at the final drug’s most resistant genotype. The problem is a finite-horizon MDP small enough to solve exactly by backward induction.

States. A genotype is a string s∈{0,1}4s\in\{0,1\}^4s∈{0,1}4, where a 1 marks the presence of a mutation, so ∣S∣=16|\mathcal S|=16∣S∣=16. The wild type is 0000. The model assumes that the population is dominated by a single genotype at all times, which is the usual regime when mutations are rare and selection is strong.

Actions. At each of the steering epochs t=1,…,N−1t=1,\ldots,N-1t=1,…,N−1 the action is one of the 15 drugs. Epoch NNN applies a fixed final drug d⋆d^\stard⋆.

Transitions. Let fa(s)f_a(s)fa​(s) be the measured growth rate of genotype sss under drug aaa, and let Ua(s)U_a(s)Ua​(s) be the set of genotypes that differ from sss in one mutation and grow faster. Under drug aaa, a single fitter mutant takes over the population with each substitution, and every fitter neighbour is equally likely to be the one that does:

Ma(j∣s)={1/∣Ua(s)∣j∈Ua(s),1j=s and Ua(s)=∅,0otherwise.M_a(j\mid s)= \begin{cases} 1/|U_a(s)| & j\in U_a(s),\\ 1 & j=s \text{ and } U_a(s)=\emptyset,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}Ma​(j∣s)=⎩⎨⎧​1/∣Ua​(s)∣10​j∈Ua​(s),j=s and Ua​(s)=∅,otherwise.​
(38)

A genotype with no fitter neighbour is a local peak of the landscape and absorbs the chain. Because each substitution strictly increases the growth rate, every path reaches a peak within 15 substitutions. A drug is given long enough for this to happen, so the transition kernel of one decision epoch is the limit of the chain, p(j∣s,a)=[lim⁡m→∞Mam]sj=[Ma16]sjp(j\mid s,a)=\big[\lim_{m\to\infty}M_a^m\big]_{sj}=[M_a^{16}]_{sj}p(j∣s,a)=[limm→∞​Mam​]sj​=[Ma16​]sj​.

Objective. Let s⋆s^\stars⋆ be the genotype with the highest growth rate under d⋆d^\stard⋆. There is no stage cost. The terminal cost is the probability that the final drug carries genotype sss to s⋆s^\stars⋆, cN(s)=p(s⋆∣s,d⋆)c_N(s)=p(s^\star\mid s,d^\star)cN​(s)=p(s⋆∣s,d⋆), and the goal is to minimize its expected value. Backward induction (Backward induction, with a minimum in place of the maximum) reads

vN(s)=cN(s),vt(s)=min⁡a∑jp(j∣s,a) vt+1(j),t=N−1,…,1.v_N(s)=c_N(s),\qquad v_t(s)=\min_{a}\sum_{j}p(j\mid s,a)\,v_{t+1}(j),\qquad t=N-1,\ldots,1 .vN​(s)=cN​(s),vt​(s)=amin​j∑​p(j∣s,a)vt+1​(j),t=N−1,…,1.
(39)

The resulting policy is Markov deterministic: one drug for each pair of epoch and genotype. Using it assumes that the dominant genotype is sequenced before each drug. Nichol et al. (2015) assume instead that nothing is observed and that the initial genotype is uniformly distributed, the worst case in which any resistant strain may already be present. Their decision rules ignore the state, so a policy reduces to a fixed sequence of drugs. Both are policies in the sense of the decision rules section, and since a fixed sequence is a Markov policy that happens to be constant in sss, backward induction can only do as well or better. The two classes also differ in cost. The best fixed sequence of kkk steering drugs is found by checking all 15k15^k15k sequences, while backward induction costs kkk products of 15 transition matrices with a 16-vector.

Without steering, ampicillin carries 62% of the starting genotypes to 1111. The best single steering drug, cefprozil, reduces this to 25%, the value reported by Nichol et al. (2015). If the genotype is observed first, the backward-induction policy reaches 11% with the same number of drugs (Figure 3). It uses four different drugs, depending on the genotype. Cefprozil can leave a population at 0101, one of its peaks, from which ampicillin climbs straight to 1111. Most genotypes from which that can happen receive cefotaxime (CTX) or ceftazidime (CAZ) instead.

With two steering drugs, the fixed sequence “ampicillin, then cefprozil” already reaches zero, and feedback has nothing left to add. Giving the final drug first sends every genotype to one of ampicillin’s three peaks, 0011, 0110 and 1111. Cefprozil then moves 1111 to 0110 and leaves the other two in place. When ampicillin is given again, the population sits on one of its two lower peaks and stays there. The first drug has made the state predictable without measuring it, which is why a sequence that ignores the state can do as well as one that observes it. The table below shows that this is the exception. For most final drugs a gap remains after three steering drugs; for cefepime (FEP) the best fixed sequence leaves a probability of 0.33 and the feedback policy 0.14.

Probability that the population ends at the most resistant genotype of the final drug, when every starting genotype is equally likely. Fixed is the best drug sequence found by exhaustive search; feedback is the backward-induction policy, which observes the genotype before each drug. Bold marks a feedback value lower than the best fixed sequence.

Two rows show the limits of steering. Ampicillin with sulbactam (SAM) has a single peak at 1111, so every population ends there whatever comes before. For ceftizoxime (ZOX) and piperacillin with tazobactam (TZP), three steering drugs remove only a fraction of the risk, with or without feedback. Another difference between the two classes does not show in the table. The backward-induction policy is computed once and applies to every starting distribution, while the best fixed sequence must be searched again whenever the prior over the starting genotype changes. Choosing the wild type as the starting population in the replay makes cefotaxime the best single steering drug. With one steering drug and a known starting genotype, there is nothing to observe before the only decision, so the fixed sequence and the policy give the same probability, 0.15.

The model is a deliberate idealization. Real populations hold several genotypes at once, drugs are given for fixed durations rather than until evolution stops, and growth rate in a laboratory culture is only a proxy for fitness in a patient. The transition matrices and the measured landscapes are nevertheless real data, and the example shows the two features that matter for the rest of the chapter: the optimal decision depends on the state, and backward induction finds it at a cost that grows linearly with the horizon.

Summary and Outlook¶

Stochastic dynamic programming separates decision rules by the information and randomization they use, then evaluates each action by averaging its continuation value over the transition kernel. Finite-horizon optimality remains a backward recursion because the terminal date supplies the boundary condition.

For continuous-time systems driven by Gaussian disturbances, the same short-time recursion gives the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation. Path-integral stochastic control examines a class of such systems for which optimal feedback can be estimated from weighted trajectories.

What replaces that boundary when decisions continue indefinitely? The infinite-horizon formulation uses discounting to obtain bounded value functions and fixed-point equations whose solutions no longer depend on a terminal time.
